query:
Context: Our lab performs standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (k-ratio protocol, NIST DTSA-II) on bulk metal samples - laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg measured at 5 kV on a Thermo Fisher (FEI) Apreo field-emission SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD (takeoff angle 35 degrees). We have an uncoated single-crystal MgO standard (an insulator), and our carbon evaporation coater is unavailable for two months. In an SEM course our team was told that the Apreo can analyze non-conductive specimens WITHOUT a conductive carbon coat by operating in variable-pressure / low-vacuum SEM (VPSEM) mode. Scope: SEM only; exclude TEM entirely.

Questions:

(1) Verify from the peer-reviewed literature: is it true that variable-pressure / low-vacuum / environmental SEM permits imaging AND X-ray microanalysis of uncoated, electrically non-conductive specimens? Explain the charge-neutralization mechanism precisely and quantitatively: ionization of chamber-gas molecules by the primary beam and by emitted secondary/backscattered electrons; drift of positive ions to the negatively charged specimen surface; the steady-state surface potential achieved (versus the kilovolt-scale negative charging of an uncoated insulator in high vacuum); typical gases (water vapor, nitrogen, air, helium) and chamber pressure ranges (roughly 10-4000 Pa); pressure-limiting apertures and differential pumping that keep the gun and column at high vacuum; and gas-cascade-amplified secondary electron detection (GSED / dedicated low-vacuum detectors) versus the Everhart-Thornley detector, which cannot operate at elevated pressure.

(2) Recommend ONE authoritative paper about VPSEM/ESEM suitable as a first read for a graduate student - ideally open access, and ideally covering X-ray microanalysis in the variable-pressure SEM since that is our application. Candidates to evaluate (do not limit yourself to these): Danilatos 1988 'Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy' (Advances in Electronics and Electron Physics 71:109-250); Thiel & Toth 2005 'Secondary electron contrast in low-vacuum/environmental scanning electron microscopy of dielectrics' (J. Appl. Phys. 97:051101); Stokes 2008 book 'Principles and Practice of Variable Pressure/Environmental Scanning Electron Microscopy (VP-ESEM)'; Newbury 2002 'X-ray microanalysis in the variable pressure (environmental) scanning electron microscope' (J. Res. NIST 107:567-603). Give the full citation with DOI for your single recommendation, state whether a free/open-access copy exists and where, and give one sentence on why it over the others.

(3) Critically for our use case: what does VPSEM/low-vacuum operation do to QUANTITATIVE energy-dispersive X-ray microanalysis? Cover the gas-scattering beam 'skirt' in detail: the fraction of primary-beam electrons scattered out of the focused probe as a function of gas species, pressure, gas path length, and beam energy (published example numbers, especially near 5 keV where elastic scattering cross sections are larger); the skirt radius (focused probe versus the hundreds-of-micrometers-to-millimeters skirt, e.g. the Danilatos oligo-scattering treatment); consequences for the spatial resolution of analysis, for minor/trace-element analysis (spurious contributions from material far from the probe), and for standards-based k-ratio quantification with measured probe current/dose (Faraday cup bookkeeping when a pressure-dependent fraction of the current is in the skirt); published mitigation and correction strategies (minimum gas path length, helium as the imaging gas, lowest workable pressure, beam-skirt correction/deconvolution models, measuring standards under identical gas conditions) and their demonstrated accuracy limits. Bottom line: does the literature support accurate standards-based k-ratio EDS quantification (few-percent relative accuracy) of a charging insulator standard such as MgO in low-vacuum mode at 5 kV, or does it recommend high vacuum plus a conductive coating for quantitative work?

(4) Briefly: vendor naming and capability landscape - Thermo Fisher/FEI 'low vacuum' mode versus ESEM (trademark; e.g. Quattro), Zeiss 'VP', Hitachi 'VP-SEM', typical maximum chamber pressures for each class, and anything published (papers, application notes cited in literature) about the Apreo platform's low-vacuum option specifically (maximum chamber pressure, whether it requires a dedicated low-vacuum detector).

For every claim cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters (e.g., the variable-pressure SEM chapter of Goldstein et al., Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, 4th edition) with DOIs, and note honestly where the literature is silent.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1

    Status:

        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?

Use the tools to answer the question: Context: Our lab performs standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (k-ratio protocol, NIST DTSA-II) on bulk metal samples - laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg measured at 5 kV on a Thermo Fisher (FEI) Apreo field-emission SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD (takeoff angle 35 degrees). We have an uncoated single-crystal MgO standard (an insulator), and our carbon evaporation coater is unavailable for two months. In an SEM course our team was told that the Apreo can analyze non-conductive specimens WITHOUT a conductive carbon coat by operating in variable-pressure / low-vacuum SEM (VPSEM) mode. Scope: SEM only; exclude TEM entirely.

Questions:

(1) Verify from the peer-reviewed literature: is it true that variable-pressure / low-vacuum / environmental SEM permits imaging AND X-ray microanalysis of uncoated, electrically non-conductive specimens? Explain the charge-neutralization mechanism precisely and quantitatively: ionization of chamber-gas molecules by the primary beam and by emitted secondary/backscattered electrons; drift of positive ions to the negatively charged specimen surface; the steady-state surface potential achieved (versus the kilovolt-scale negative charging of an uncoated insulator in high vacuum); typical gases (water vapor, nitrogen, air, helium) and chamber pressure ranges (roughly 10-4000 Pa); pressure-limiting apertures and differential pumping that keep the gun and column at high vacuum; and gas-cascade-amplified secondary electron detection (GSED / dedicated low-vacuum detectors) versus the Everhart-Thornley detector, which cannot operate at elevated pressure.

(2) Recommend ONE authoritative paper about VPSEM/ESEM suitable as a first read for a graduate student - ideally open access, and ideally covering X-ray microanalysis in the variable-pressure SEM since that is our application. Candidates to evaluate (do not limit yourself to these): Danilatos 1988 'Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy' (Advances in Electronics and Electron Physics 71:109-250); Thiel & Toth 2005 'Secondary electron contrast in low-vacuum/environmental scanning electron microscopy of dielectrics' (J. Appl. Phys. 97:051101); Stokes 2008 book 'Principles and Practice of Variable Pressure/Environmental Scanning Electron Microscopy (VP-ESEM)'; Newbury 2002 'X-ray microanalysis in the variable pressure (environmental) scanning electron microscope' (J. Res. NIST 107:567-603). Give the full citation with DOI for your single recommendation, state whether a free/open-access copy exists and where, and give one sentence on why it over the others.

(3) Critically for our use case: what does VPSEM/low-vacuum operation do to QUANTITATIVE energy-dispersive X-ray microanalysis? Cover the gas-scattering beam 'skirt' in detail: the fraction of primary-beam electrons scattered out of the focused probe as a function of gas species, pressure, gas path length, and beam energy (published example numbers, especially near 5 keV where elastic scattering cross sections are larger); the skirt radius (focused probe versus the hundreds-of-micrometers-to-millimeters skirt, e.g. the Danilatos oligo-scattering treatment); consequences for the spatial resolution of analysis, for minor/trace-element analysis (spurious contributions from material far from the probe), and for standards-based k-ratio quantification with measured probe current/dose (Faraday cup bookkeeping when a pressure-dependent fraction of the current is in the skirt); published mitigation and correction strategies (minimum gas path length, helium as the imaging gas, lowest workable pressure, beam-skirt correction/deconvolution models, measuring standards under identical gas conditions) and their demonstrated accuracy limits. Bottom line: does the literature support accurate standards-based k-ratio EDS quantification (few-percent relative accuracy) of a charging insulator standard such as MgO in low-vacuum mode at 5 kV, or does it recommend high vacuum plus a conductive coating for quantitative work?

(4) Briefly: vendor naming and capability landscape - Thermo Fisher/FEI 'low vacuum' mode versus ESEM (trademark; e.g. Quattro), Zeiss 'VP', Hitachi 'VP-SEM', typical maximum chamber pressures for each class, and anything published (papers, application notes cited in literature) about the Apreo platform's low-vacuum option specifically (maximum chamber pressure, whether it requires a dedicated low-vacuum detector).

For every claim cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters (e.g., the variable-pressure SEM chapter of Goldstein et al., Scanning Electron Microscopy and X-Ray Microanalysis, 4th edition) with DOIs, and note honestly where the literature is silent.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Accurate analyses are also demonstrated for interferences involving large concentration ratios: a major constituent on a minor constituent (Ba at 0.4299 mass fraction on Ti at 0.0180) and a major constituent on a trace constituent (Ba at 0.2194 on Ce at 0.00407; Si at 0.1145 on Ta at 0.0041). Accurate analyses of low atomic number elements, C, N, O, and F, are demonstrated. Measurement of trace constituents with limits of detection below 0.001 mass fraction (1000 ppm) is possible within a practical measurement time of 500 s.

Abstract:
The relatively recent entry of field emission electron microprobes into the field of microanalysis provides another tool for the study of small features of interest (e.g., mineral and melt inclusions, ex-solution lamellae, grain boundary phases, high-pressure experimental charges). However, the critical limitation for accurate quantitative analysis of these submicrometer- to micrometer-sized features is the relationship between electron beam potential and electron scattering within the sample. To achieve submicrometer analytical volumes from which X-rays are generated, the beam accelerating voltage must be reduced from 15–20 to ≤10 kV (often 5 to 7 kV) to reduce the electron interaction volume from ~3 to ~0.5 μm in common geological materials. At these low voltages, critical Kα X-ray lines of transition elements such as Fe are no longer generated, so L X-ray lines must be used. However, applying the necessary matrix corrections to these L lines is complicated by bonding and chemical peak shifts for soft X-ray transitions such as those producing the FeLα X-ray line. It is therefore extremely challenging to produce accurate values for Fe concentration with this approach. Two solutions have been suggested, both with limitations. We introduce here a new, simple, and accurate solution to this problem, using the common mineral olivine as an example. We also introduce, for the first time, olivine results from a new analytical device, the Extended Range Soft X-ray Emission Spectrometer.

Abstract:
Background For decoding the mechanism of how cells and organs function information on their ultrastructure is essential. High-resolution 3D imaging has revolutionized morphology. Serial block face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM) offers non-laborious, automated imaging in 3D of up to ~ 1 mm^3 large biological objects at nanometer-scale resolution. For many samples there are obstacles. Quality imaging is often hampered by charging effects, which originate in the nonconductive resin used for embedding. Especially, if the imaged region of interest (ROI) includes the surface of the sample and neighbours the empty resin, which insulates the object. This extra resin also obscures the sample’s morphology, thus making navigation to the ROI difficult. Results Using the example of small arthropods and a fish roe we describe a workflow to prepare samples for SBF-SEM using the minimal resin (MR) embedding method. We show that for imaging of surface structures this simple approach conveniently tackles and solves both of the two major problems—charging and ROI localization—that complicate imaging of SBF-SEM samples embedded in an excess of overlying resin. As the surface ROI is not masked by the resin, samples can be precisely trimmed before they are placed into the imaging chamber. The initial approaching step is fast and easy. No extra trimming inside the microscope is necessary. Importantly, charging is absent or greatly reduced meaning that imaging can be accomplished under good vacuum conditions, typically at the optimal high vacuum. This leads to better resolution, better signal to noise ratio, and faster image acquisition. Conclusions In MR embedded samples charging is minimized and ROI easily targeted. MR embedding does not require any special equipment or skills. It saves effort, microscope time and eventually leads to high quality data. Studies on surface-linked ROIs, or any samples normally surrounded by the excess of resin, would benefit from adopting the technique.

Abstract:
Hypoxia triggers activation of platelets, leading to thrombosis. If not addressed clinically, it can cause severe complications and fatal consequences. The current treatment regime for thrombosis is often palliative and include long-term administration of anticoagulants, causing over-bleeding risk and other secondary effects as well. This demands a molecular understanding of the process and exploration of an alternative therapeutic avenue. Interestingly, recent studies demonstrate that platelets exhibit functional autophagy. This cellular homeostatic process though well-studied in non-platelet cells, is under-explored in platelets. Herein, we report autophagy activation under physiologically relevant hypoxic condition (10% O2; associated with high altitude) in ex-vivo platelets and in vivo as well. We show that autophagy inhibition using chloroquine (CQ), a repurposed FDA-approved drug, can significantly reduce platelet activation, both in ex-vivo and in-vivo settings. Further, surgical ligation of inferior vena cava (IVC) was performed to induce thrombus formation. Interestingly, CQ pre-treated rats showed reduced clotting ability in surgical animals as well. Importantly, thrombosis inhibitory dose of CQ was considerably lower than the currently used drug-acetazolamide; CQ was also found to be non-toxic to the tissues. Hence, we propose that repurposing of CQ can attenuate hypoxia-induced thrombosis through inhibition of autophagy and can be explored as an effective therapeutic alternative.

Abstract:
An anti-oxidant Cu layer was achieved by remote mode N2 plasma. Remote mode plasma treatment offers the advantages of having no defect formation, such as pinholes, by energetic ions. In this study, an activated Cu surface by Ar plasma chemically reacted with N free radicals to evenly form Cu nitride passivation over the entire Cu surface. According to chemical state analysis using XPS, Cu oxidation was effectively prevented in air, and the thickness of the Cu nitride passivation was within 3 nm. Based on statistical analysis using the DOE technique with N2 plasma variables, namely, RF power, working pressure, and plasma treatment time, we experimentally demonstrated that a lower RF power is the most effective for forming uniform Cu nitride passivation because of a lower plasma density. When the N2 plasma density reached approximately 109 cm−3 in which the remote mode was generated, high energy electrons in the plasma were significantly reduced and the amount of oxygen detected on the Cu surface was minimized. Finally, low temperature (300 °C) Cu–Cu bonding was performed with a pair of the anti-oxidant Cu layers formed by the remote mode N2 plasma. Cu atomic diffusion with new grains was observed across the bonded interface indicating significantly improved bonding quality over bare Cu–Cu bonding.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'he2003astudyof pages 16-24'.

J He. A study of the electron beam scattering under various gaseous environment. Unknown journal, 2003.

In variable-pressure or environmental SEM, the residual gas provides charge carriers that reduce insulating-specimen charging. Primary electrons, secondary electrons, and backscattered electrons collide with gas molecules and generate positive and negative ions, as well as additional electrons liberated in subsequent ionizing collisions. The electric field produced by the charged specimen and electrode bias accelerates charged particles, promoting further gas ionization and an avalanche-like cascade. Secondary electrons emitted from the specimen are identified as the major contributor because of their low energy, while positive ions have much greater mass and lower mobility than electrons; ion–gas collisions therefore contribute significantly to the cascade. The resulting ion current compensates the specimen’s charge: positive ions drift toward negatively charged surface regions, and negative ions toward positively charged regions. This feedback tends to neutralize local charge buildup rather than allowing the specimen potential to rise indefinitely. According to the excerpt, introducing gas lowers the surface potential at all incident beam energies from typically thousands of volts in high vacuum to approximately a few hundred volts in a gaseous environment. The excerpt does not provide a universal exact steady-state potential; it indicates that the final value depends on conditions such as gas pressure, beam energy, charging, and electrode bias, with a representative low-vacuum range of a few hundred volts.

The excerpt describes charge neutralization as a gas-ionization compensation process in variable-pressure SEM. Primary electrons strike the insulating specimen, producing secondary electrons; these emitted electrons ionize gas molecules above the surface. The ionization efficiency depends on secondary-electron yield, which varies with specimen material, surface roughness, and beam energy. At sufficiently low pressure, the specimen becomes negatively charged relative to ground, creating an electric field that accelerates the positively charged gas ions toward the surface. If the ions travel far enough to gain energy, they can produce further ionization in a cascade; the likelihood of this depends on gas pressure, electric field, and gas path length. As pressure increases, more positive ions reach the specimen and compensate its negative charge. Once the surface potential approaches zero, the electric field weakens or disappears, suppressing the ion cascade. The steady state is therefore approximately zero surface potential, or slightly positive when incoming ion flux exceeds the remaining negative charging. The final state reflects competition among incident primary electrons, emitted secondary electrons, gas ionization, and electron–positive-ion recombination. Higher beam energy reduces secondary-electron yield and therefore reduces the available ion flux for compensation.

In variable-pressure or environmental SEM, the primary electron beam, together with emitted secondary electrons (SE) and backscattered electrons (BSE), ionizes gas molecules in the chamber through electron–molecule collisions. The resulting gas avalanche includes positive and negative ions, electrons liberated in ionizing collisions, and electrons generated when positive ions strike the specimen. Secondary electrons are particularly important because their low energy gives them a high interaction cross section. Charging of an insulating specimen and any electrode bias establish an electric field that drives the charge carriers: positive ions migrate toward negatively charged specimen regions, while negative ions move toward positive regions. Positive-ion impact and the resulting ion current compensate surplus negative charge, lowering the specimen’s surface potential and reducing charging. As pressure rises, ionization and charge neutralization initially become stronger; however, positive-ion/electron recombination increasingly suppresses the avalanche. The surface potential therefore does not decrease indefinitely. At a pressure-dependent steady state, gas-ionization compensation is balanced by recombination and ongoing beam-induced charging, producing a stabilized surface potential. The excerpt describes this as a dynamic equilibrium or stabilization state, with its value depending on pressure, gas species, beam energy, electrode bias, and specimen conditions.

Scanning, 29 3:114-22, May 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.20052, doi:10.1002/sca.20052. This article has 15 citations.

The excerpt establishes that the beam skirt is a major limitation for quantitative EDS in VP-SEM/ESEM. Gas scattering causes primary electrons to spread outside the focused beam, producing X-rays from regions beyond the intended analysis point; consequently, measured spectra may not represent the material of interest. The skirt radius increases with gas pressure and working distance, and decreases as accelerating voltage increases. Gas composition also matters: helium produces the smallest skirt among the gases compared in the excerpt. These effects imply degraded spatial resolution and potential errors in measurements of small features, interfaces, particles, and minor or trace constituents, although the excerpt does not give detailed numerical effects on k-ratios or detection limits. Standards-based quantification can therefore be biased unless the skirt contribution is removed or corrected; the excerpt specifically discusses pressure-variation correction methods rather than providing a complete k-ratio treatment. Mitigation includes higher accelerating voltage, lower pressure, minimizing the electron path length through gas (including shorter working distance), and selecting helium where practical. The Doehne and Gauvin pressure-variation methods reportedly gave results within 10% of measurements at 0 Pa, with the Gauvin method described as more user-friendly and precise over the full pressure range. Thus, accurate low-vacuum k-ratio EDS is possible with appropriate corrections, but the excerpt does not establish uncorrected accuracy.

At the specimen surface, the beam consists of an unscattered Gaussian component with reduced intensity and a scattered, spatially extended “skirt”; skirt enlargement may reach several hundred micrometers. This broadens the effective excitation region and degrades interface/profile spatial resolution and contrast, making small compositional variations difficult or impossible to resolve. It is believed that this goal can be achieved by integrating the electron

   The simple analysis presented above becomes in practice very complex

## pqac-00000035

From text 'staniewicz2012transmissionmodeimagingin pages 36-43'.

Transmission-mode imaging in the environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt explains that ESEM maintains a high-vacuum electron gun and electron-optics column alongside a much higher-pressure specimen chamber through differential pumping. Because the electron source operates around 10^-5–10^-8 Pa while the chamber may reach about 2660 Pa, one pump is insufficient. Instead, multiple pressure-limiting apertures (PLAs) separate successive pumping stages. The first PLA, where the beam enters the specimen chamber, is typically 300 or 500 µm in diameter; a second 300 µm PLA is positioned above it, with the intervening region pumped to roughly 10 Pa. Further stages progressively reduce pressure up the column, using rotary or scroll pumps in higher-pressure regions, diffusion or turbomolecular pumps at intermediate pressures, and ion-getter pumps near the gun. Each aperture sharply restricts gas flow, confining most gas near the chamber and minimizing beam-gas scattering and resolution loss. The gas path length (GPL) is defined as the distance from the first PLA to the specimen and, together with chamber pressure, determines the amount of gas encountered by the beam. The supplied excerpt does not state typical numerical GPL values, so those would require another source.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'danilatos1988foundationsofenvironmental pages 21-25'.

G.D. Danilatos. Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy. Advances in electronics and electron physics, 71:109-250, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6, doi:10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6. This article has 676 citations.

The excerpt describes pressure-limiting apertures (PLAs) as thin-wall apertures used to separate the elevated-pressure specimen region from the high-vacuum electron-optics column in ESEM. Gas enters through the first aperture (PLA1), passes through the inter-aperture region, and is restricted again by PLA2 before reaching the electron column. The apertures’ conductance controls the gas leak, and differential pumping removes the transmitted gas. Pump performance and pipe/aperture conductances are compared to determine whether a section is pump-limited or conductance/pipe-limited. The text reports measurements of aperture conductance for air: the proportionality constant was approximately 149.6 m/s over 1–100 kPa, close to the theoretical value, with approximately 152 m/s at 100 kPa and 141 m/s at 5 kPa. PLA geometry and positioning are critical because a gas jet from PLA1 can strike PLA2 and send substantially more gas into the electron-optics column. Experiments mapped pressure contours and identified a hollow region of the jet where PLA2 could be positioned to reduce leakage. The excerpt does not specify the absolute gas-path lengths or typical PLA spacing; it only states that the aperture separation was chosen greater than the jet length in the cases discussed.

## pqac-00000037

From text 'danilatos1988foundationsofenvironmental pages 67-71'.

G.D. Danilatos. Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy. Advances in electronics and electron physics, 71:109-250, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6, doi:10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6. This article has 676 citations.

The excerpt presents ESEM as using at least two pumping stages and three pressure regions, separated by pressure-limiting apertures (PLA1 and PLA2). These apertures restrict gas flow from the elevated-pressure specimen chamber toward the electron-optics column, while the pumping stages remove the gas that passes through, allowing the chamber to operate from vacuum up to 100 kPa (one atmosphere) while maintaining much lower pressure upstream. The stated prototype has an electron-optics-column pressure that is poorly preserved in the OCR, an intermediate pressure of approximately 10 Pa between PLA1 and PLA2, and a specimen-chamber range from vacuum to 100 kPa. The excerpt also provides relevant geometric path lengths: PLA1 and PLA2 are separated by approximately 8 mm, and PLA1 is approximately 2.1 mm from the wire/specimen edge. In the beam-profile experiment, the electron beam travels 370 micrometres after reaching the wire edge before collection; this is a local beam path rather than the full gas-transfer path. The passage indicates that pressure regions and apertures also affect beam scattering and collection efficiency, but it does not give a complete general design definition or all typical PLA dimensions.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'staniewicz2012transmissionmodeimagingin pages 43-48'.

Transmission-mode imaging in the environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt identifies pressure-limiting apertures (PLAs) as apertures in the electron-beam path that, together with pumping stages, separate the elevated-pressure specimen chamber from the much lower-pressure microscope column. It specifically states that the first PLA–pump system reduces pressure by approximately a factor of one hundred, illustrating differential pumping: gas is allowed in the final chamber, while successive apertures and pumps restrict its flow toward the gun and column and maintain their high-vacuum conditions. The gas burden affecting the beam is governed mainly by final-chamber pressure and the gas path length (GPL), defined here as the distance from the first PLA to the specimen. GPL is not necessarily identical to working distance because apertures may extend beyond the polepiece. A shorter GPL and lower chamber pressure reduce electron beam spreading; the specimen can be moved closer to the first PLA, generally by raising the stage. The excerpt does not provide numerical typical GPL values. It notes that specialized conical PLAs are available where a fixed polepiece-to-sample working distance is required, such as for EDX analysis.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'staniewicz2012transmissionmodeimagingin pages 32-36'.

Transmission-mode imaging in the environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt describes pressure-limiting apertures (PLAs) and differential pumping as the central engineering features that permit ESEM operation with gas in the specimen chamber while protecting the electron source and beam path. PLAs restrict gas flow from the elevated-pressure specimen region toward the electron gun and column, while differential pumping removes the gas that does pass through successive apertures, maintaining the high-vacuum conditions needed for electron generation and transport. The historical account states that Danilatos and Robinson introduced this arrangement in 1979, enabling imaging in an atmosphere. It also notes that commercial ESEMs generally operate below atmospheric pressure, with FEI instruments reaching approximately 20 Torr (2666 Pa), whereas the minimum pressure for sustaining liquid water is about 4.5 Torr (600 Pa) at 0°C. The excerpt identifies the existence and purpose of PLAs and differential pumping, but it does not provide numerical dimensions for the apertures, the number of pumping stages, or typical gas path lengths between apertures and the specimen. Therefore, specific PLA-to-specimen or chamber-to-gun path-length values cannot be obtained from this passage.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'danilatos1988foundationsofenvironmental pages 10-14'.

G.D. Danilatos. Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy. Advances in electronics and electron physics, 71:109-250, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6, doi:10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6. This article has 676 citations.

The excerpt describes pressure-limiting apertures (PLAs) as small apertures that restrict gas flow and sustain a pressure difference between adjacent regions of an ESEM/VP-SEM. Rather than using a window or film, the aperture method is preferred because films introduce substantial electron scattering, can fail from beam damage or puncture, and may not withstand the required pressure difference. Differential pumping is represented as a two-stage pressure-reduction system: gas enters from an external source, passes through a controlled leak or needle valve into the specimen chamber, and then flows through successive apertures, pipes, and pump stages toward the high-vacuum side. The article uses an electrical-circuit analogy in which pressure corresponds to voltage, gas flow or leak rate to current, and apertures and pipes to resistors; conductance and pump speed determine the resulting intermediate pressures. For small PLA conductances, pressure reduction improves with smaller apertures and larger pump/pipe conductances. However, aperture size cannot be reduced indefinitely because of electron-optical limitations and field-of-view restrictions. The supplied pages do not state typical gas-path lengths; they only discuss pipes, apertures, and the two-stage arrangement qualitatively.

## pqac-00000041

From text 'danilatos1988foundationsofenvironmental pages 14-17'.

G.D. Danilatos. Foundations of environmental scanning electron microscopy. Advances in electronics and electron physics, 71:109-250, Jan 1988. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6, doi:10.1016/s0065-2539(08)60902-6. This article has 676 citations.

The excerpt discusses the pressure-management principle underlying ESEM/VP-SEM: pressure is divided into successive pumping stages, with pressure-limiting apertures (identified in the text as PLA1) restricting gas flow between regions. It states that a third pressure-limiting stage may be needed when the first two stages cannot provide sufficiently high vacuum for LaB6 or field-emission guns, while two stages using rotary and oil-diffusion pumps can achieve very low pressure in the gun area, allowing a tungsten filament to operate for its expected life. The PLA does not simply eliminate gas flow; its conductance controls the leak rate, and the resulting flow can include a downstream gas jet and upstream streaming or depletion. The excerpt explains that aperture and pipe conductance depends on the flow regime: in free-molecular flow, the mean free path exceeds the aperture or pipe dimension and conductance is pressure-independent; at higher pressure, viscous flow becomes relevant. These restrictions, combined with separate pumping stages, allow the specimen-side region to remain relatively elevated in pressure while progressively protecting the electron column and gun. However, the supplied pages do not provide a clear definition of the complete differential-pumping layout or numerical typical gas-path lengths; they only discuss aperture/tube geometry and conductance generally.

## pqac-00000044

From text 'zoukel2014minesdouaicrp pages 113-116'.

A ZOUKEL. Mines douai crp tudor fnr luxembourg universite de lille. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt identifies Newbury (2002) among studies addressing beam-skirt complications in VP-SEM X-ray microanalysis. It describes the principal mechanisms affecting EDS: the primary beam undergoes elastic scattering in the environmental gas, producing a non-focused skirt, while inelastic interactions with gas atoms generate characteristic and bremsstrahlung X-rays. Consequently, environmental-gas peaks appear in the EDS spectrum and increase with pressure. Scattering also reduces the beam current delivered to the focused probe at the specimen, lowering the intensity of peaks from the material of interest and degrading lateral spatial resolution. X-rays generated by remotely scattered skirt electrons are indistinguishable from those generated by the focused probe, reducing the signal-to-spurious-intensity ratio. The excerpt presents pressure-variation approaches associated with Newbury and others: spectra acquired at different pressures can be compared or subtracted to estimate the zero-scattering/zero-pressure spectrum; a related method extrapolates intensity against the unscattered beam fraction. It notes that results depend on suitable pressure and accelerating-voltage choices. The thesis proposes minimizing skirt degradation by selecting conditions for which the skirt radius RS is no greater than the intrinsic X-ray emission radius RX (RS ≤ RX).


---

## pqac-00000045

From text 'mansour2020environmentalgasimpact pages 1-6'.

O. Mansour, N. Lateb, A. Zoukel, Z. Hafsi, A. Kadoun, and L. Khouchaf. Environmental gas impact on the emission volume of x-rays near the interface in the variable pressure scanning electron microscopy. Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultramic.2019.112920, doi:10.1016/j.ultramic.2019.112920. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt cites Newbury (2002) as a source concerning the additional analytical problems encountered in variable-pressure or environmental SEM/EDS compared with conventional high-vacuum SEM/EDS. It characterizes the central issue as scattering of the incident electron beam by the chamber gas. The scattered electrons form a broad “beam skirt” around the focused probe and can generate X-rays outside the intended interaction region, including signals from nearby materials with different compositions. Consequently, EDS measurements may contain spurious or extraneous X-ray contributions that are difficult to distinguish from X-rays generated directly under the probe. The excerpt states that increasing gas pressure makes environmental-gas-related X-ray signals more detectable, while electron scattering reduces the current remaining in the focused beam and lowers the target-material peak intensity. These combined effects degrade X-ray spatial or lateral resolution, compromise signal-to-spurious intensity ratios, and limit the quality and interpretation of qualitative and quantitative microanalysis. The broader paper also notes that beam-skirt effects motivated correction approaches such as beam-stop and pressure-variation methods, although these attempt to separate skirt and primary-beam components rather than eliminate the underlying problem.

## pqac-00000046

From text 'zoukel2014minesdouaicrp pages 192-192'.

A ZOUKEL. Mines douai crp tudor fnr luxembourg universite de lille. Unknown journal, 2014.

This excerpt is not the Newbury (2002) NIST Journal of Research paper, so it does not establish exactly what that paper covered or report its specific numerical findings. It is, however, closely relevant to the question because it describes the same variable-pressure/environmental SEM problem: gas molecules scatter the primary electron beam, producing a beam “skirt.” The skirt introduces artifacts in imaging and chemical microanalysis and degrades the spatial resolution that would otherwise be defined by the high-vacuum interaction volume. The stated research goals were to determine the skirt’s magnitude and spatial extent and to develop a methodology for mitigating its effect. The excerpt says that experimental parameters can be quantified in terms of their impact on spatial-resolution degradation. It also presents a low-vacuum interaction volume, formed by both scattered and unscattered electron-beam fractions, as the basis for preserving high-vacuum-like spatial resolution. The keywords specifically identify X-ray microanalysis, EDS profiles, point analysis, line scans, interfaces, and X-ray absorption/secondary fluorescence. These themes can help contextualize Newbury’s discussion of how beam skirt broadening causes EDS signals to originate outside the nominal probe position, thereby limiting microanalytical spatial resolution, but the excerpt itself does not provide Newbury’s detailed findings.

Robert A. Carlton. The effect of some instrument operating conditions on the x-ray microanalysis of particles in the environmental scanning electron microscope. Scanning, 19:85-91, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950190205, doi:10.1002/sca.4950190205. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt is from Carlton’s 1997 study rather than Newbury’s 2002 NIST Journal of Research paper, so it does not directly document what Newbury’s paper covered. It nevertheless provides closely related background on beam-skirt effects in variable-pressure or environmental SEM. The study examined how accelerating voltage, chamber pressure, detector type, and working distance affect particle EDS spectra. Gas scattering broadens the incident electron beam, producing a skirt that can irradiate neighboring particles, the substrate, and mounting materials. Consequently, substrate peaks appeared in nearly all spectra, while neighboring-particle peaks varied with operating conditions. The largest contamination from neighboring particles occurred with the GSED at 21.5 mm working distance, 10 kV, and 665 Pa. Fewer artifacts were observed using the long ESD at 19 mm working distance and low pressure. The excerpt also cites evidence that particles millimeters away can contribute counts, and that increasing pressure substantially increases beam scattering. It supports minimizing gas path length and pressure while maximizing accelerating voltage, and recommends the long ESD with a 19 mm working distance for EDS. These findings may help contextualize Newbury’s discussion of beam-skirt limitations, but the excerpt does not establish Newbury’s specific conclusions.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000053

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Testing the accuracy of low-beam-energy electron-excited x-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry. Journal of Materials Science, 59:19088-19111, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that low-beam-energy EDS at an incident beam energy of 5 keV achieved high overall accuracy. The study analyzed 263 concentrations covering 39 elements in 113 materials using the standards-based k-ratio protocol and NIST DTSA-II software. Accuracy was characterized by relative deviation from expected value (RDEV): more than 98% of measurements were within ±5% RDEV, and 82% were within the narrower −2% to +2% RDEV interval. The excerpt establishes 5 keV as the lowest beam energy considered capable of producing a useful characteristic X-ray for all elements except hydrogen and helium. The tested materials included NIST microanalysis-suitable SRM glasses and alloys, Fe3C, reagent compounds such as BaTiO3, PbS, and MoS2, stoichiometric compounds such as TiN, TiO2, and Cr2N, and minerals. MgO is not specifically listed in the provided pages, although Mg-containing glasses and other oxides were included; the excerpt alone cannot confirm whether MgO itself was tested. Experimental operating conditions such as high-vacuum status and how beam current was measured are not provided in this excerpt and would require later methods sections.

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Testing the accuracy of low-beam-energy electron-excited x-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry. Journal of Materials Science, 59:19088-19111, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

For DTSA-II low-beam-energy EDS analyses at E0 = 5 keV, the study reports 263 concentration measurements covering 39 elements in 113 materials. More than 98% of the atomic-concentration results were within ±5% relative deviation from the expected value (RDEV), and 82% were within −2% to +2% RDEV. The authors state that this RDEV distribution was similar to that obtained using conventional analysis at E0 ≥ 10 keV. Results for characteristic X-ray energies below 1.5 keV and those from 1.5–5 keV were also described as very similar. The tested challenge compositions included oxides, along with borides, carbides, nitrides, and fluorides, particularly involving low-energy peaks below 1 keV. However, this excerpt does not identify MgO specifically, nor does it provide the experimental operating conditions requested—such as high-vacuum status, measured beam current, or current-measurement procedure. It also reports that raw analytical totals at 5 keV ranged from 0.8 to 1.2, with 67% between 0.95 and 1.05. A separate 122-analysis dataset achieved 100% within ±5% RDEV and 89% within ±2% RDEV.

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 14-16'.

Journal of Materials Science, 59:19088-19111, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt contains Table 1 results for analyses identified as 5 keV and performed on the TESCAN_EDAX analytical platform. It shows several measures of deviation from reference values rather than a single overall accuracy figure. In the displayed rows, normalized-concentration RDEVs include 0.09%, 0.61%, and 0.90%, while atomic-concentration RDEVs include 0.19%, −0.40%, −0.12%, and 0.53%. Raw-concentration RDEVs in the same portion range from −5.0% to +2.4% (with additional displayed values between these limits), indicating generally small deviations for these examples. The table explicitly includes MgO standards multiple times, as well as SiO2 and Al2O3; other listed standards include GaP, CaF2, K411, and K412. The sample-preparation text states that all raw materials were materialographically prepared, fine powders were mounted in conducting epoxy, and non-conductive materials received an approximately 10 nm carbon coating. The excerpt does not specify whether the measurements were made under high vacuum, nor does it describe how beam current was measured. It also does not provide a complete RDEV distribution across the entire study, so broader accuracy statistics would require other pages or sections.

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Testing the accuracy of low-beam-energy electron-excited x-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

These pages describe the measurement and data-processing methodology but do not report the numerical accuracy achieved at 5 keV or the distribution of relative deviation error (RDEV). The excerpt indicates that materials were screened for surface contamination: AlN was excluded because carbon and oxygen increased as beam energy decreased, whereas Au40-Cu60 was considered acceptable because only a small relative increase in C and O was observed. MgO was explicitly included among the stoichiometric compound standards, along with FeS2 and KCl, for elements whose pure forms were unsuitable because of instrument-vacuum incompatibility or beam instability. Measurements used either a JEOL 8500F EPMA or a TESCAN MIRA3 LMU SEM, each with alternative silicon-drift EDS configurations. Quantification used standards-based k-ratios and DTSA-II, with XPP matrix corrections and absorption coefficients from Chantler’s FFAST database (and Sabbatucci’s MACs where applicable). The database description says beam current was monitored throughout each measurement sequence and standards were used to ensure constant dose. However, the excerpt does not specify the actual high-vacuum setting, beam current value, or whether all 5-keV measurements were made under high vacuum. The requested accuracy and RDEV results likely appear later in the article.

From text 'newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 22-24'.

Dale E. Newbury and Nicholas W. M. Ritchie. Testing the accuracy of low-beam-energy electron-excited x-ray microanalysis with energy-dispersive spectrometry. Journal of Materials Science, 59:19088-19111, Oct 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-10285-4. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not report the study’s numerical accuracy result at 5 keV, the RDEV distribution, whether MgO or specific oxide standards were included, or the operating conditions such as vacuum level and beam-current measurement method. It does state that low-beam-energy operation reduces the absorption correction and therefore reduces RDEV, and that selected low-energy lines are expected to be more accurate at 5 keV than at higher beam energies because the electron beam penetrates less deeply. For the 5-keV measurements, the raw analytical total (the sum of measured mass concentrations, including assumed-stoichiometry constituents) was used as an internal consistency indicator. Unlike conventional-beam analyses, where totals generally fall between 0.98 and 1.02, the 5-keV totals had a much broader distribution: most clustered near unity, but values from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 occurred. The excerpt emphasizes that these totals are not themselves an accuracy or RDEV distribution. It also cautions that practical unknowns may contain oxide, sulfide, or other surface layers that compromise accuracy by creating a nonuniform interaction volume. Sequentially lowering beam energy from at least 10 keV to 5 keV or below was recommended to reveal such surface anomalies.
